transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-07-14 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Lena Ortiz (Redwood AE), Daniel Park (Redwood SE), Aisha Rahman (Orion, Head of ML), Tom Becker (Orion, CTO), Maya Singh (Orion, Platform Eng)

[00:00] Lena: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh this is Lena from Redwood, we've got Daniel on the line to go through the hosted API demo for chat and text generation basics. how's everyone doing?
[00:20] Aisha: Good, thanks - excited to see streaming and, um, how retries work. we have some latency SLOs so wanna understand tradeoffs.
[00:30] Tom: yeah, quick note - we're deciding between hosted and dedicated, so any comments on predictable throughput vs cost would be helpful.
[00:40] Daniel: totally, we'll cover that. quick agenda: streaming, request params, retries/backoff and idempotency, and then security. we'll show a quick live curl and SDK example.

[02:05] Daniel: okay starting with streaming - Redwood supports chunked streaming where tokens come in as they're generated, so you can render partial responses in the UI. it's standard server-sent events style or websocket from SDKs.
[02:30] Aisha: does streaming reduce end-to-end latency or just perceived latency?
[02:38] Daniel: mostly perceived latency — you start getting tokens earlier. it also helps with UX for long replies. backend latency per token is the same but you can render progressively. also we have prefix/KV caching which reduces token compute on repeated prompts. sometimes transcription says "kay vee cache" but it's the KV cache.

[04:12] Lena: quick qual: what's your typical seq length and QPS?
[04:19] Maya: so, typical request is around 120-200 tokens, peak spikes to 300 qps for a short period, sustained ~50 qps, and p95 latency target is under 250ms for chat completions.
[04:40] Daniel: okay that'll be helpful for the pilot script — we'll simulate bursts and steady load.

[06:40] Daniel: request params — key knobs are temperature (0-1), top_p, max_tokens, and presence/frequency penalties. recommended defaults for deterministic escapes are temp 0.0-0.2. higher temps for creative.
[07:05] Aisha: do you support partial / streaming token-level metadata? like token provenance or logprobs?
[07:15] Daniel: yes, logprobs are available but cost/latency increases; streaming logprobs is possible but not recommended at very high QPS.

[10:00] Tom: on retry semantics — what's Redwood's recommended pattern if the request times out?
[10:08] Daniel: we recommend idempotency keys for safe retries, exponential backoff, and small number of retries for non-idempotent flows. for hosted API we support 409/5xx semantics; SDK automatically retries on transient errors with jitter. also we include a response header with request-id so you can correlate.
[10:45] Aisha: do retries re-run the model or is there dedupe on our side?
[10:50] Daniel: retries will re-run unless you use idempotency keys; with idempotency the platform dedupes or returns the previous result if it's still available.

[15:00] Daniel: demo time — curl example: POST /v1/generate with stream=true, send temp=0.2, max_tokens=256. show partial SSE output coming back — small lag at the start while kernels warm up, then token chunks.
[15:35] (demo shows streaming tokens, Lena narrates)
[16:10] Maya: I noticed a small startup latency — is there warm pool for hosted?
[16:20] Daniel: yes, hosted uses a warm pool with continuous batching. for very latency-sensitive workloads Dedicated or reserved capacity can keep kernels hot and reduce tail latency; we also offer burst credits.

[20:00] Tom: security — SOC2 is a must, and we also need KMS integration for key control and audit logs. can you walk through that?
[20:12] Lena: yep. Redwood is SOC2 compliant, we support customer-managed keys via KMS/HSM integrations, and full audit logs with retention options. we'll share the SOC2 + security whitepaper after call.
[20:35] Aisha: what about SSO and RBAC? we need SAML SSO for console access and role separation.
[20:45] Daniel: SAML/SSO is supported for the console, and RBAC with fine-grained roles for API keys + tokens. for Private deployments we support VPC peering and on-prem packaging.

[25:00] Maya: any concerns about PCI scope? we're a payments company — we need to minimize scope and ensure we don't log sensitive card text.
[25:20] Lena: understood — we have redaction patterns, tokenization guidance, and you can opt to disable retention for certain endpoints. Redwood Hosted offers options to not persist prompts, or you can use Dedicated/Private for full data isolation.

[30:00] Daniel: on cost controls — per-token pricing for hosted, and reserved capacity for Dedicated. Redwood Optimize gives batching and quantization recommendations to lower unit cost. we can run a cost projection based on your qps and sequence lengths.
[30:30] Tom: curious about quantized models — how much performance loss vs cost savings?
[30:38] Daniel: usually 4-bit quantization can get near FP16 quality with big savings, but it depends on model and evals. Redwood Optimize will recommend quant profiles by workload.

[35:00] Aisha: for the pilot — can we run a short benchmark with our prompts and compare p95 and token-cost across streaming and non-streaming?
[35:12] Lena: yes — Daniel will share a benchmark harness and a script. we'll also include sample SDK snippets for node/python and a curl example for streaming.

[40:00] (Speaker 1): quick Q about rate limiting — what's default and can we get higher quotas during rollout?
[40:10] Daniel: default quotas depend on account tier; we can provision burst capacity for the pilot and increase rate limits for demo. also support request routing by region to reduce latency.

[45:00] Lena: recap — we'll send pricing + burst vs dedicated comparison, security docs, and the benchmark script. next step is the pilot next week pending Maya's QPS profile.
[45:20] Maya: I'll send the QPS profile and a sample prompt set by end of day tomorrow.
[46:00] Tom: thanks, appreciate the detail.
[46:20] Aisha: one more — about SDKs: any differences in streaming behaviour between node and python?
[46:28] Daniel: minor differences in client APIs, but streaming semantics are consistent. we'll add code snippets.
[47:10] Lena: great — thanks everyone. we'll follow up with the deck and docs.
[47:50] (call ends)
